Kfcfbb077 is "Static and Dynamic Analysis of Electrostatically Actuated MEMS Shallow Arches for Various Air-Gap Configurations" (Micromachines 2021). Full text. It discusses that instability occurs when attractive force > elastic restoring force, snap vs pull-in distinction; and shapes (ARC, COSINE, V) affect it; and "co-existence of states under the same actuating force". A key line: "When the DC amplitude surpasses a threshold value where the attractive force is greater than the movable micro-beam elastic restoring force, an instability occurs making the deformable electrode to either snap ... or to pull-in". That's force-controlled criterion. Also earlier quote: "for the case of lower actuation, the snap-through threshold voltage grows with the increase in the mid-point's initial rise value and decrease of the effective length".

Relevant bits for my gap: the criterion is stated as force vs restoring force, i.e., load-control; the distinction snap-through vs pull-in is the analogue of "two different instabilities with different thresholds" — like my "release (snap) vs continuous branch". And note it's "under the same actuating force" co-existence → hysteresis loop.

Now, my "control stiffness" idea: is it supported/undermined? The arch literature (electrostatic) is load-controlled (voltage → force), so snap happens. My device is displacement-controlled via a rod-on-spring, so the fold can be regularized. The bent-sheet paper: displacement-controlled shear u and still gets snap-through — because the shear is applied to a rigidly clamped edge, but the sheet's internal negative stiffness makes the branch unstable at fixed u as well? Hmm. With rigid displacement control of a single scalar u, the equilibrium path can still fold in u (turning point) even with perfect displacement control; snap occurs at a limit point in u. So displacement control doesn't generically remove the jump — it only removes jumps caused by force-control limit points. Important correction! In my device, γ is the rod displacement, but the rotor connects through a spring; the rotor angle θ is not directly controlled, so θ can jump while γ stays smooth. Right: the jump is in θ at fixed γ; the fold condition is ∂²U/∂θ² = 0 with γ as parameter. That's exactly the saddle-node in θ; the control stiffness k_d shifts the fold location but the fold still exists generically. A "continuous route" then requires the fold to be destroyed (branch merge / imperfect bifurcation), not mere finite stiffness. However, with finite k_d, near the fold, the equilibrium branch in θ can be continuous but extremely steep — no, at a saddle-node the branch ceases to exist, and beyond it no nearby equilibrium → dynamic jump. The jump size is small near the fold merger but nonzero; the "silent segment" slope is finite.

So: my earlier v2 idea (band = near-threshold where the continuous branch exists and jump→0) — the "stiffness" language: the fold merger occurs when the constraint manifold's two saddle-nodes collide (in θ-γ plane). The distance from merger controlled by (x_offset, R−ℓ0) etc. The load-control vs displacement-control distinction is a separate, second mechanism: whether the driving spring's stiffness matters for where the fold sits. Actually with finite k_d, the total potential includes the drive spring; the fold of ∂²U/∂θ²=0 depends on k_d. So the band boundary moves with k_d. That is a genuine, checkable claim: "the same rotor geometry can snap or not depending on k_d" — i.e., the map (x_offset, R−ℓ0) alone doesn't fix the boundary; there's a third axis: stiffness ratio k_c/k_d? Hmm, careful: does k_d change whether a fold exists? Yes: with a very soft drive spring, the rotor sees a nearly dead load, and the equilibrium set is the same as the constraint branch's equilibria (fold at the constraint's own limit). With a stiff drive spring, the drive term adds positive curvature k_d(∂γ/∂θ)² — so the total curvature can stay positive even where the constraint has negative curvature; the fold then shifts to a different γ and the jump size shrinks. So k_d moves and shrinks the jump but does not eliminate the fold (the constraint's negative stiffness grows without bound away from the stop). Fine.

So the dimensionless distance parameter: the fold is where ∂²U_c/∂θ² = −k_d L² cos²θ. So there's a one-parameter family boundary in the plane of negative stiffness vs k_d L². That gives the dimensionless criterion: Ω ≡ k_d L² cos²θ_stop / |K_neg^max|. When Ω>1, the constraint branch is stabilized over the whole range where it exists → no snap, continuous. When Ω<1, snap. Where |K_neg^max| = max negative stiffness of the constrained branch. Near the "threshold" of the stop constraint (i.e., where the branch barely exists), |K_neg^max| → 0, hence Ω → ∞, so continuous. That reproduces the near-threshold continuity and gives the concrete control parameter: ratio of control stiffness to maximum negative stiffness.

That is a real improvement: it replaces "distance to threshold" with a ratio of two stiffnesses which are both computable from apparatus geometry (k_d, L, k_c, ℓ, mounting). And it makes a concrete prediction: rotating the drive spring stiffness k_d (e.g., using S046 vs S007 for the drive spring!) changes the silent-segment width and jump height, without moving the geometric threshold configuration. apparatus has driving_k 0.19 N/cm for both pairs; but calibration springs S046=0.46, S019=0.19, S007=0.07 N/cm exist. Interesting: the calibration sample stiffness nominal values are 0.46, 0.19, 0.07 N/cm — and pair_A driving_k is 0.19. So swapping drive springs is a natural variation the calibration table supports! That's a nice concrete consequence: the drive spring stiffness axis is already realized in the calibration samples, and the coupling spring pair_A is 0.07.

Wait: coupling_k = 0.07 N/cm for pair_A; and rest lengths 2.4/2.6; so coupling is soft relative to drive. That matters for the ratio: the coupling stiffness sets |K_neg| near the shared-node fold. k_c/k_d = 0.07/0.19 ≈ 0.37.

Hmm, but careful: for a single rotor, the negative stiffness at the stop-bound branch comes from the driving spring's own geometry (L·cosθ term), not k_c. The "constraint torque" arises because the stop blocks motion; the constrained rotor's total torque balance determines equilibrium. As the other rotor is fixed at its stop, coupling torque is roughly constant → no negative stiffness from coupling. Negative stiffness appears when the coupling force depends on θ (spring length changes nonlinearly). Fine — the specifics can be left qualitative.

So the conceptual move for this step could be:

"释放的连续/跳变不是由「到阈值的几何距离」单独决定，而是由一个控制刚度比 Ω = k_d L² (∂θ/∂γ)² / |K_neg| 决定；Ω>1 时约束支被整流化为连续支（跳变消失），Ω<1 时跳变大小随 Ω 减小而增大。因此近阈值带不是几何带，而是「几何给负刚度、刚度给控制」的乘积带；同一几何换驱动弹簧即换带。"

This is a solid relation with concrete consequences and it uses the returned sources: Kfcfbb077's "attractive force > elastic restoring force" criterion (load-controlled threshold; snap vs pull-in as two instabilities), K233c25's "minimum dimensionless stiffness β ... sufficient axial force", K1f367e2's thickness-independent geometric criterion u_c = 0.06/L̄ (a challenge: geometry-only criterion at large aspect ratio → my Ω might be wrong in那个 regime; but the sheet's control is rigid displacement and it still snaps at a geometric threshold; that's a caution that when negative stiffness is geometric, the threshold can be geometry-only, and the jump/continuity is different).

Also the ±1 coarse-graining gap: the play/stop model (K1364a25, Df33e048) — play operators have continuous output and still possess congruency + wiping-out; so a continuous branch coexists with RPM. And Kd215cb: ρ permutation governs graph topology, |R| = # of increasing subsequences in ρ — RPM organizes the graph. Combined: the "order" parameter ρ is about sequences of switching events, not about the value of states. So ±1 coarse-graining is legitimate for the topology question as long as (i) each event is a full switch between branches, and (ii) a "continuous branch" segment doesn't produce spurious events. But if a rotor is on a continuous branch, its "state" is a function of γ, so the return map is no longer piecewise constant → the graph loses its discrete structure; the correct coarse-graining is to keep the sequence of extrema (reversal points), which is exactly the play-model state. So: the minimal state set should be "±1 contact sign + continuous offset" — hmm, that's already in my question. The learning: the play model gives exactly the mathematical form for that: state = set of past reversal points; equivalently, output = clamp(input, [u−r, u+r]) — so the continuous amplitude lives in the widths r, and the state is the "last extremum" (a continuum). Meanwhile the Preisach model = distribution of relays with ±1 outputs. So the two models are structurally the same family with continuous vs discrete output. That means: my worry "±1 coarse-graining loses the amplitude" is real for the state alphabet but the memory structure (which extremum is retained) is unaffected — return-point memory is about the last reversal values, so it survives coarse-graining of the amplitude as long as the output map remains monotone in the retained state. This gives a conditional claim: RPM survives amplitude coarse-graining iff the coarse-grained output map is well-defined as a function of the retained reversal sequence (i.e., amplitude is slaved to γ, not independent).

Good: two conceptual connections, both grounded.
